text: Hello, this is Grete. The casket is open, and the night is not over yet. Peter has things to hand out, and a long, dark walk lies ahead for the Rosens. You’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 11, and study one sentence the way a writer does. Today’s question: what does it cost to do the brave thing, even when it works?

Today’s reading move asks you to be a little choosy. Not everything is a symbol, and a reader who calls everything a symbol isn’t really reading. Ask one question about each object you notice: does anyone in the story care about it? If nobody does, it’s probably there to help you see the room.

The model is about Peter, and a promise he can’t quite make. The sentence to fix is really two sentences run together, and each one has two words pressed into one. Find where the first thought ends. Then give the second thought a capital to stand on.

Today the word work moves from noticing to using. You’ve found the patterns. Now you put them to work: choosing when to press two words together, and splitting long words in the right place. A writer chooses on purpose. That’s what you’re practicing here.

Halfway through the woods now. The path is darker here, under the trees. Four more words with the go-roots. One of them is the opposite of coming closer, like the tide pulling back from the beach. As you work, listen to each ending before you choose.

Match these four again, and this time, say each word out loud in a sentence about Chapter 11 before you tap. If you can use a word, you own it. If you can only recognize it, it still belongs to the book.

Here you get to choose. Pressing two words together changes how a sentence sounds, like the difference between a person talking and a sign on a wall. Fill in each blank. Then, in the last line, listen for whose voice you hear: a person, or a notice pinned to a door.

Clap each word before you type anything, and count the claps. Then check your split against your claps. If your split makes a beat you didn’t clap, something’s wrong. Your ears are the best spelling check you have.

Today’s Courage Watch is about letting go. When the Jewish family upstairs from us left in October 1943, they left the dishes on the table. Mrs. Levin pressed a little brass key into my mother’s hand and said, keep it for us. Watch the Rosens in this chapter. Notice what they had to leave behind, and what they carry with them anyway.

Read slowly when the casket is opened. Watch what Peter takes out, and what he gives to each person. Notice the tiny passenger who needs something to keep her warm. And notice a small packet that changes hands without anyone explaining it. Ask yourself why nobody asks.

Read this sentence aloud and feel where it slows down. Right in the middle, a little mark tells you a list is coming. Then three places, one after another, like steps. Ask why Lowry stops at three. Would two be enough? Would four be too many?

Now you write. The questions ask about the packet Peter hands over, what the candlesticks stood for, and what Annemarie asks Peter when he says goodbye. Then, in your essay, you’ll tie each body paragraph back to your big idea with one strong closing sentence.

Be careful with the third question. Peter does say goodbye. But Annemarie answers him with a question, and his answer is only half an answer. Think about what nobody could promise anybody in October 1943. That’s where your thinking should start.

Each body paragraph needs a knot at the end, or the thread slips out. Today you add one closing sentence to each paragraph, using a key word from your claim. It’s a small sentence, but it reminds your reader why the whole paragraph matters.

Every Friday evening, the family upstairs lit two candles in silver candlesticks a lot like these. I could see the glow under their door when I passed on the stairs. When they had to leave, the candlesticks stayed behind on the table. Years later, they told me those were the first thing they thought about in Sweden. Not their beds. The candlesticks.
Succeed. To do well, to do what you set out to do.
Recede. To go back, the way the tide does.
Process. Steps that go forward, one after another.
Secede. To break away from a group.
